stimulus.title: Exercício D1: psicologia (meta de 4 min)
stimulus.content:
Narrator: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.

Professor: We've been discussing decision-making, and today I want to bring up something researchers call the paradox of choice. The idea is counterintuitive: you'd think more options would always make us happier, but past a certain point it does the opposite.

A classic example. In one well-known study, researchers set up a tasting table in a grocery store: first with six varieties of jam, then with twenty-four. You'd expect the bigger display to sell more. Actually, the smaller display generated significantly more purchases. The larger one attracted more browsers, but far fewer of them bought anything.

Why? Two things: decision fatigue and anticipated regret. With more options, comparing them mentally becomes exhausting — that's the fatigue. And even before you pick, you start worrying that one of the other twenty-three might be better and that you'll regret your choice — that's the regret. Ironically, more choices can leave people stuck at square one, unable to commit at all.

Now, this doesn't mean choice is bad: a complete absence of options is its own problem. The point is there's a sweet spot, and past it, additional options stop helping and start working against us. To be fair, later studies haven't always replicated the jam result, so the size of the effect is still debated.

prompt: Gist-content. What is the talk mainly about?

options.A: Grocery stores should minimize the products they display
options.B: Beyond a point, more options can reduce satisfaction and hinder decisions
options.C: Consumers always prefer smaller displays
options.D: Decision fatigue affects only in-store shoppers

explanation: Tese anunciada no início e no fechamento. (A) exagera; (C) também exagera ("always") e generaliza um único estudo; (D) está fora do que foi dito.

stimulus.title: Exercício D2: biologia (meta de 4 min)
stimulus.content:
Narrator: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.

Professor: When we picture a forest, we tend to see individual trees competing — for light, for water, for space. And that's real. But over the last thirty years, research has revealed something the old picture missed: the trees are also connected, underground, through fungi.

Here's how. The roots of most trees are wrapped in a network of fungal threads; this partnership between root and fungus is called a mycorrhiza. The fungi pull in water and minerals the tree's roots can't reach efficiently, and hand them to the tree. In return, the tree gives the fungi sugars it makes through photosynthesis. So far, a simple trade.

The surprising part is that a single fungal network can link many trees at once — even trees of different species. And things move along those links. Experiments using radioactive tracers have shown carbon flowing from a tree standing in full sun to a shaded seedling of another species nearby. Some researchers describe old, well-connected trees as "hub trees" that support younger ones around them.

Now, a word of caution. This work has captured the public imagination, and some popular accounts overstate it: talking about forests as single cooperative organisms. The jury's still out on how deliberate or widespread the sharing really is. What's solid is that the connections exist and that resources can move through them. How much that reshapes our model of the forest is still being worked out.

prompt: Gist-content. What is the main point of the talk?

options.A: Trees in a forest only compete, never cooperate
options.B: Trees are connected underground through fungal networks, and resources can move between them
options.C: Mycorrhizal fungi are harmful to most trees
options.D: Forests are single cooperative organisms

explanation: O professor admite a competição mas acrescenta a conexão. (A) ignora a segunda metade da tese; (C) é o oposto (a relação é benéfica); (D) é exatamente o exagero que ele critica no fim.

stimulus.title: Exercício D3: história da tecnologia (meta de 4 min)
stimulus.content:
Narrator: Listen to part of a talk in a history of technology class.

Professor: Look at your keyboard. The top row of letters spells Q-W-E-R-T-Y. It's an odd arrangement — the most common letters aren't under your strongest fingers. So why has it survived, essentially unchanged, for a hundred and fifty years?

The layout dates from the 1870s, from early mechanical typewriters. The common story is that QWERTY was designed to slow typists down so the metal type-bars wouldn't jam. That's probably an oversimplification (the real design pressures were more mixed), but the key point is that the layout was shaped by the constraints of 1870s machinery, constraints that vanished decades ago.

Better layouts have been proposed. The best known, Dvorak, was patented in 1936 and, in some studies, allows modestly faster and more comfortable typing. Yet it never caught on. Why not?

This is a textbook case of what economists call path dependence, or sometimes "lock-in." Once QWERTY became the standard, everything organized itself around that standard: typewriters were built for it, typing was taught on it, and every new typist learned it because that's what the machines used — and machines used it because that's what typists knew. To switch, a single person gains little unless nearly everyone switches at once. The cost of coordinating that switch is enormous, and no one bears it. So an arrangement that made sense only for 1870s hardware is still, quietly, on every device you own.

prompt: Gist-content. What is the talk mainly about?

options.A: How to type faster using the Dvorak layout
options.B: Why an outdated keyboard layout has persisted, as an example of path dependence
options.C: The mechanical design of 19th-century typewriters
options.D: Why Dvorak is objectively the best possible layout

explanation: A pergunta central é por que um layout ultrapassado sobreviveu, e a resposta é path dependence. (A)/(D) mudam o foco/exageram; (C) é contexto, não o tema.

stimulus.title: Exercício D4: zoologia (meta de 3 min)
stimulus.content:
Narrator: Listen to part of a talk in an introductory zoology class.

Professor: All right, let's continue our unit on marine mammals. Last time we talked about whales, which spend their whole lives in deep water. Today, I want to look at a much smaller animal that lives right along the rocky coast: the sea otter.

Unlike seals, which come onto the beach to rest, sea otters do almost everything in the water. They hunt there, they eat there, and, believe it or not, they even sleep floating on their backs. Now, that creates a pretty obvious problem. The ocean is always moving. If you fall asleep floating on the surface, the waves and currents can easily push you out into the open sea, away from your food and your group.

So how do sea otters solve this? Well, they use a clever trick. Before going to sleep, an otter swims into a bed of giant kelp, which is a tall kind of seaweed anchored to the ocean floor. The otter wraps a few long strands of kelp around its body like a blanket. That keeps it in one place while it naps.

And if there's no kelp nearby, otters sometimes hold paws with another otter so they don't drift apart. It looks cute to us, of course, but for the otters, it's really a practical survival habit.

prompt: Gist-content. What is the main topic of the talk?

options.A: How sea otters hunt for food along rocky coastlines
options.B: How sea otters avoid drifting away while sleeping in the ocean
options.C: Why giant kelp forests are disappearing from coastal waters
options.D: Why sea otters spend more time on beaches than seals do

explanation: O foco da aula é mostrar como as lontras-marinhas dormem na água sem serem levadas pela correnteza: "If you fall asleep floating on the surface, the waves and currents can easily push you out... So how do sea otters solve this?" A opção (A) pega uma palavra isolada do começo, mas a caça não é desenvolvida na explicação.

stimulus.title: Exercício D5: história da arquitetura (meta de 4 min)
stimulus.content:
Narrator: Listen to part of a talk in an architectural history class.

Professor: When we think about keeping buildings cool in desert climates, we usually picture modern air-conditioning units humming away on every wall. But people have lived comfortably in hot, dry regions for thousands of years without electricity. A great example of how they did it is the windcatcher, or badgir, a tower structure perfected in ancient Persia.

If you look at the skyline of an old desert city like Yazd, in modern-day Iran, you'll see dozens of these rectangular towers rising above the flat roofs. At the top of each tower, there are vertical openings facing the prevailing wind. Even a light breeze high above the street gets caught by these openings and funneled straight down into the living spaces below.

Now, what happens when there's no wind at all? Well, that's where the design gets really clever. Without a breeze, the tower works like a chimney. Engineers call this a solar chimney. The sun heats the south side of the tower, warming the air inside it. Because warm air rises, it flows up and out through the top of the tower. That pulls cooler air from shaded courtyards or underground water channels into the rooms downstairs.

stimulus.title: Exercício D6: psicologia cognitiva (meta de 4 min)
stimulus.content:
Narrator: Listen to part of a talk in a cognitive psychology class.

Professor: Have you ever noticed that when you're studying for an exam, the one practice problem you couldn't finish keeps popping into your head at dinner, while the ten problems you solved easily just fade away? There's actually a name for that: the Zeigarnik effect.

It goes back to the 1920s. A psychologist named Bluma Zeigarnik was sitting in a busy Berlin restaurant with her professor and some classmates. She noticed something odd about the waiters. A waiter could remember a long, complicated order for a big table without writing anything down. But the moment the food was served and the bill was paid, if you asked that same waiter what the table had ordered, he had no idea. He'd wiped it clean from his memory.

Curious, Zeigarnik went back to her lab and gave volunteers a series of simple tasks, like solving puzzles or stringing beads. Here's the catch: she interrupted them halfway through some of the tasks and let them finish the others. Later, when she asked them to list all the tasks they'd worked on, people were about twice as likely to remember the ones they hadn't finished.

Her explanation was that starting a task creates a kind of mental tension, almost like an open tab on your computer browser. That tension keeps the information active and easy to recall until the job is done. Once you finish, the tab closes, and your brain lets go.

options.A: Waiters have better short-term memory than most university students
options.B: Interruptions during study sessions permanently damage long-term recall
options.C: Writing down tasks is less effective than memorizing them mentally
options.D: People tend to remember unfinished tasks better than completed ones

explanation: A aula gira em torno do efeito Zeigarnik, segundo o qual lembramos melhor de tarefas inacabadas do que das já concluídas: "people were about twice as likely to remember the ones they hadn't finished." A alternativa (A) foca apenas na história dos garçons, que serve para mostrar como a psicóloga teve a ideia inicial.

stimulus.title: Exercício D7: economia comportamental (meta de 4 min)
stimulus.content:
Narrator: Listen to part of a talk in a behavioral economics class.

Professor: In standard economic theory, rational decision-makers look only at future costs and benefits. Whatever money, time, or effort you've already spent and can't recover is called a sunk cost, and logically, it shouldn't influence what you do next. Yet in real life, we let sunk costs drive our choices all the time.

Picture this: you buy a nonrefundable twenty-dollar ticket to an outdoor concert. The evening of the show, a freezing rainstorm rolls in. You're miserable just thinking about going. If the ticket had been free, you'd stay home on the couch without a second thought. But because you paid twenty dollars, you drag yourself out into the rain so you don't "waste" the ticket. See the flaw? The twenty dollars is gone either way. By going, you haven't saved your money; you've just traded a dry evening for a wet, miserable one.

And it's not just individuals who fall into this trap. Governments and corporations do too. In fact, economists sometimes call this the Concorde fallacy, after the supersonic passenger jet developed jointly by Britain and France. Long before the plane entered service, both governments realized it would never make back its massive development costs. Walking away would have saved billions. Instead, neither side wanted to admit that the money already spent was lost, so they kept pouring funds into the project for years.

Why is it so hard to walk away? Partly because of loss aversion: we hate admitting a loss more than we enjoy an equivalent gain. Once we recognize that bias, though, we can ask a simpler question: if I were starting from scratch today, would I still invest in this?

options.A: How airline companies calculate ticket prices for international flights
options.B: Why people and organizations continue investing in losing endeavors
options.C: Why outdoor events should always offer refundable tickets to buyers
options.D: How Britain and France competed to build the fastest passenger aircraft

explanation: A palestra analisa a falácia dos custos irrecuperáveis, mostrando por que pessoas e governos insistem em escolhas ou projetos que já deram prejuízo: "Whatever money, time, or effort you've already spent and can't recover is called a sunk cost... we let sunk costs drive our choices all the time." stimulus.title: Exercício D8: linguística histórica (meta de 4 min)
stimulus.content:
Narrator: Listen to part of a talk in a historical linguistics class.

Professor: We often treat dictionary definitions as if they were carved in stone, and people love to complain when a word starts being used in a new way. But to a linguist, semantic shift—the gradual change in a word's meaning over time—isn't a corruption of language; it's one of its most predictable features. Today I want to focus on two opposite directions this shift can take: amelioration, where a word's meaning becomes more positive, and pejoration, where it becomes more negative.

Take the ordinary English word "nice." If someone calls your essay "nice" today, it's a mild compliment. But if we trace "nice" back to its Latin root, nescius, it meant "ignorant" or "unaware." When it entered Middle English through French, it meant "foolish" or "silly." Over the next few centuries, though, its meaning softened: from foolish to shy, then to fussy or fastidious, then to precise and delicate, and finally to pleasant and agreeable. That upward climb from "ignorant" to "pleasant" is a classic case of amelioration.

Now look at the reverse trajectory: pejoration. Consider the word "silly." In Old English, its ancestor, saelig, meant "blessed" or "happy." Over time, because blessed, innocent people were seen as harmless and defenseless, the word shifted to mean "deserving of pity," then "weak," and eventually "foolish" or "lacking common sense." So while "nice" climbed the social ladder, "silly" slid down it.

Notice what drives both shifts. Words don't change meaning in a vacuum; they shift because speakers stretch them in everyday conversation—through irony, politeness, or exaggeration—until the new implication replaces the old core meaning entirely.

options.A: To argue that modern dictionaries should preserve original Latin meanings
options.B: To explain how French grammar reshaped Middle English sentence structure
options.C: To illustrate how words can shift toward more positive or negative meanings
options.D: To show why formal academic writing avoids informal adjectives like "nice"

explanation: O objetivo da aula é explicar e exemplificar duas direções da mudança semântica, para sentidos mais positivos ou mais negativos: "amelioration, where a word's meaning becomes more positive, and pejoration, where it becomes more negative." A opção (A) vai contra a visão da professora logo no primeiro parágrafo.

Now look at the reverse trajectory: pejoration. Consider the word "silly." In Old English, its ancestor, saelig, meant "blessed" or "happy." Over time, because blessed, innocent people were seen as harmless and defenseless, the word shifted to mean "deserving of pity," then "weak," and eventually "foolish" or "lacking common sense." So while "nice" climbed the social ladder, "silly" slid down it.

Notice what drives both shifts. Words don't change meaning in a vacuum; they shift because speakers stretch them in everyday conversation—through irony, politeness, or exaggeration—until the new implication replaces the old core meaning entirely.

Today I want to focus on two opposite directions this shift can take: amelioration, where a word's meaning becomes more positive, and pejoration, where it becomes more negative.

Take the ordinary English word "nice." If someone calls your essay "nice" today, it's a mild compliment. But if we trace "nice" back to its Latin root, nescius, it meant "ignorant" or "unaware." When it entered Middle English through French, it meant "foolish" or "silly." Over the next few centuries, though, its meaning softened: from foolish to shy, then to fussy or fastidious, then to precise and delicate, and finally to pleasant and agreeable. That upward climb from "ignorant" to "pleasant" is a classic case of amelioration.

Now look at the reverse trajectory: pejoration. Consider the word "silly." In Old English, its ancestor, saelig, meant "blessed" or "happy." Over time, because blessed, innocent people were seen as harmless and defenseless, the word shifted to mean "deserving of pity," then "weak," and eventually "foolish" or "lacking common sense." So while "nice" climbed the social ladder, "silly" slid down it.

stimulus.title: Listen to an Academic Talk (2)
stimulus.content: **TRANSCRIÇÃO (trecho de aula, Introdução à Biologia):** "So far we've treated the cell membrane as a simple barrier, but that picture is misleading. The membrane is better thought of as a busy checkpoint. It's selectively permeable — some molecules, like oxygen and carbon dioxide, pass through freely; others, like glucose or charged ions, can only cross with help, through specific protein channels or pumps. And here's the key point for today: some of those pumps run *against* the concentration gradient. They move a substance from where it's scarce to where it's already abundant, which costs energy. This is called active transport, and it's how a nerve cell, for example, maintains the sharp difference in ion concentration across its membrane that makes a nerve impulse possible."

stimulus.title: Listen to an Academic Talk
stimulus.content: **TRANSCRIÇÃO:** "Let's turn to a phenomenon economists call 'loss aversion' — the tendency for people to feel the pain of a loss more intensely than the pleasure of an equivalent gain. Classic experiments show that people who have just been given an object typically demand roughly twice as much to give it up as others are willing to pay to acquire it — a pattern known as the endowment effect. This has real consequences outside the lab. Investors, for instance, often hold onto losing stocks far longer than rational analysis would justify, simply because selling would mean formally realizing the loss. The discomfort of that realization outweighs, for many people, the objective financial logic of cutting their losses early."

options.B: People being indifferent between gains and losses of equal size
options.C: Investors always selling stocks at a loss immediately
options.D: A tendency to overvalue new purchases over old ones
